
=================================================================
#31 Four Dragons  (643 February)
Arc: Part II — The Dawn of War / The Seventh Invasion · place: changan · tone: imperial war council
Logline: The Heaven-Sent General. The Khan of Heaven. He has many names, and he is running out of countries.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ In Chang’an there is one word nobody says. It is the emperor’s name.
[1] ¶ He never quite forbids it. The two characters of his given name simply vanish from the empire, quietly: a ministry renamed because one of them sat in its title, a bodhisattva’s name shortened by a syllable, scribes copying old books leaving one stroke off — and everyone understands.
[2] ¶ He has plenty of other names, and those you may say all day. The Heaven-Sent General. The Khan of Heaven.
[3] ¶ Tell that to a herald from Samhan. Watch his face.
[4] The Herald: …They don’t say his name? At all?
[5] Chu Suiliang: Nor written, sir. We leave off a stroke. / It saves everyone a great deal of trouble.
[6] ¶ So the Second Emperor of the West is a man who has not heard another person say his own name since he was crowned, and there is nobody left alive who is allowed to.
[7] ── SCENE: The Sickroom ──
[8] ¶ The Imperial Minister is dying. At the foot of the bed the court diarist, Chu Suiliang, writes down everything the emperor says.
[9] [CARD The Imperial Minister: The emperor’s minister. His job is to say no, and he is very good at his job.]
[10] The Imperial Minister: Your Majesty. When I am gone, there will be no one left to tell you no.
[11] The Second Emperor: Why else do you think I put up with you for twenty years.
[12] The Second Emperor: With bronze for a mirror, a man straightens his robes. / With history for a mirror, he sees the rise and fall of states. / With a man for a mirror, he sees his own faults. / …Today I lose one of my mirrors.
[13] ¶ All that month the eastern reports keep coming in. In Goryeo, a king has been murdered by his own minister.
[14] The Second Emperor: Gai Suwen. / I have been turning that name over for a month. It does not get any sweeter.
[15] ¶ Chang’an writes the name without the Yeon. Yeon was the given name of the emperor’s late father, so the word is gone from the palace. A whole family loses its surname to a dead man’s dignity. It is an old family, too. Older than Goguryeo, if you ask them. They will tell you anyway.
[16] The Second Emperor: The King of Goryeo was a friend I valued. / His name… ah… / …Yeongnyu! King Yeongnyu!
[17] ¶ Everything is in place. It has been for some time; he was simply waiting to be bored enough.
[18] Chu Suiliang: Majesty, we have invaded six times already — and you would go again?
[19] The Second Emperor: Because I have not gone myself. / Life is not theory. It is practice.
[20] ── SCENE: The Third Leg ──
[21] ¶ In the third month an envoy arrives from Pyongyang with a request nobody in the Ministry of Rites has seen before. The new master of Goguryeo would like some Daoists.
[22] Goguryeo envoy: The Mangniji says a cauldron stands on three legs. / We have the Buddha. We have Confucius. / He would like the third leg, if the Son of Heaven can spare one.
[23] The Second Emperor: He wants Laozi? / Give him Laozi. Our house descends from the old man anyway. Let Goguryeo bow to my ancestor and call it theology.
[24] ¶ Eight Daoists go east with a copy of the _Daodejing_. In Pyongyang the Mangniji gives them lodgings, and the lodgings he gives them are temples. The monks are moved out the same week, with their bells.
[25] ¶ A young monk named **Shinsung** carries the smallest bell down the hill himself, to a lesser house that has no frame to hang it from, and sets it on the floor. He does not complain to anyone. The bell stays on the floor for twenty-five years.
[26] ❝QUOTE (Nirvana Sutra (大般涅槃經) fasc. 14, Noble Practice (聖行品), tr. Dharmakṣema · T12n0374, pp. 450a, 451a · Sanskrit: the same verse in the Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra (Waldschmidt ed.)) [Shinsung]: All conditioned things are impermanent; this is the law of arising and passing away. … When arising and passing away have themselves passed away, that stillness is bliss.❞
[27] ── SCENE: Three Choices ──
[28] ¶ In the ninth month an envoy comes from Silla, which is losing fortresses to Baekje faster than it can count them, and asks for an army. The Second Emperor offers him a choice of three.
[29] The Second Emperor: One. I send the Khitan and the Mohe into Liaodong, and Goguryeo looks north for a year. / Two. I give you a few thousand red coats and Tang banners. Stand them on your walls. Baekje will think I have come, and run. / Three.
[30] The Second Emperor: Your country is ruled by a woman, and your neighbours despise you for it. That is why they keep coming. / I could send you one of my own clan to be your king, with a few soldiers to look after him. When the country is safe, you may have it back.
[31] ¶ The envoy says yes, and then no, and then nothing at all. The emperor watches him for a while.
[32] The Second Emperor: A mediocre man. Not the sort a country sends when it is drowning.
[33] ¶ The report reaches Surabol in the twelfth month. The Harmony Council has the third option read aloud twice. **Bidam** reads it once, and folds it small.
[34] Bidam: He offers us a king the way a temple puts out rice for a stray. / …And there are men in this hall who would bow for the bowl.
[35] ── SCENE: Five Hundred Li ──
[36] ¶ In the new year the emperor sends a man to Pyongyang to tell Goguryeo to leave Silla alone. Gesomun receives him standing up, and does not offer a mat.
[37] Tang envoy: The Son of Heaven asks that Goguryeo stop troubling Silla. / They are his vassals. As you are.
[38] Yeon Gesomun: Vassals. Ha! / When the Sui were sitting on our chest, Silla crept in and took five hundred li of our land. / Give back the dirt. Then talk to me about peace.
[39] Tang envoy: That was long ago. Why quarrel over old things?
[40] Yeon Gesomun: Old? / It’s dirt. Dirt doesn’t get old, you fool. / Go tell him that. Use small words.
[41] ¶ The envoy carries it west word for word. The Second Emperor has it read to him twice and smiles. A refusal in writing is worth an army. Now he can raise one.
[42] ── SCENE: The Muster ──
[43] ¶ He launches the Seventh Invasion of Goguryeo. It’s the seventh army out of the West, and the first he leads himself. The clerks need three days to read the muster aloud. Horse from the frontier. Foot from the rivers. Five hundred hulls riding low with a year of grain.
[44] [EDICT Handwritten edict to the realm [The Second Emperor] (Zizhi Tongjian (資治通鑑) bk. 197, Tang Taizong, Zhenguan 18 (644), eleventh month · cf. Samguk Sagi bk. 21 (以理乘亂)): Gesomun of Goguryeo has murdered his lord and savages his people. Who could bear it? We mean to ride out to You and Ji and call Liao and Jie to account. Wherever We camp or halt, let nothing be wasted and no one be burdened. … Emperor Yang of Sui was cruel to those beneath him, and the king of Goguryeo was kind to his people. An army that longed for revolt struck a people at peace, and so it failed. Now, in short, there are five ways We are certain to win. One: the great strikes the small. Two: the loyal punishes the rebel. Three: order rides down disorder. Four: the rested meets the weary. Five: the glad meets the bitter. Why fear we will not prevail? Tell it to all the people. Let no one doubt, and no one be afraid.]
[45] ¶ Four dragon banners go up over the muster: white, red, blue and black.
[46] [CARD Blue Dragon: The Blue Dragon. The emperor’s most patient general, which is its own kind of danger.]
[47] ¶ The fifth banner has no name on it at all. Everyone knows whose it is.
[48] [MAP 645 The Seventh Invasion: Three roads in and five hundred hulls. Goguryeo’s wall was built to stop one army at a time.]
[49] ¶ Two of the four dragons were born on the steppe. The Red Dragon keeps felt tents inside the capital walls and sleeps better in them. The White Dragon walked his whole tribe across the border as a boy. He has been proving it was worth it ever since. The Black Dragon is the empress’s brother. He argued against this war in council. He’s riding to it anyway.
[50] ── SCENE: Longmen Field ──
[51] ¶ In a poor field at Longmen, a farmer named Xue Rengui is planning to rebury his ancestors. Millet, rammed earth, a hut that doesn’t pretend to be anything. He has the right soil for graves. He doesn’t yet know he has the wrong year for quiet.
[52] [CARD Xue Rengui: A poor farmer with good soil for graves. His wife thinks he could do better.]
[53] ¶ The cloth on his back is plain yellow peasant hemp, the cheapest dye the village still sells, the colour of millet at the wrong hour. He hoes. His wife, **Liu**, keeps the hut door.
[54] ¶ The Son of Heaven is calling up troops for Liaodong. The edict reaches villages that have never seen a palace, and wives who have never left the furrow.
[55] ¶ The edict comes on red paper, pasted to the well-house wall at the height of a man’s eyes: SERVE THE EMPEROR. Under it, in smaller characters, the quota. It does not ask for him by name. It asks for one man from every household with the right number of hands, and any man with hands will do.
[56] Xue Rengui: The mounds… they’re not done. / Not the dirt. The hands. / The edict — I heard it. I did.
[57] [CARD Lady Liu: A farmer’s wife. The farmer has no idea what she has planned for him.]
[58] Lady Liu: Mounds don’t wait because a man is short of hands. / And the edict doesn’t wait either. / You’re not a hoe. You’re a ji. As far as I can tell.
[59] Xue Rengui: The ji is in the shed. / The yellow clothes are here. / Liu. If I go — this door.
[60] Lady Liu: I’ll shut the door. / Don’t you start worrying about doors. / Talent needs its hour. If this is the hour — then go.
[61] ¶ He goes. She is right, and a man who can lift a **ji** should not spend the invasion stacking earth for the dead.
[62] Xue Rengui: …Ancestors. Wait a little longer. / Until I come back carrying this ji. / The yellow clothes — I’ll leave them here.
[63] ¶ He presents himself to general **Zhang Shigui** and signs his name under the Tang muster. The clerk writes _Xue Rengui_. The clerk does not look up. History will.
[64] ¶ **Yodong has never opened its gates to the West. Not for the Sui. Not in three summers. Here come the dragons…!**

=================================================================
#32 Yodong  (645 May)
Arc: Part II — The Dawn of War / The Seventh Invasion · place: yodong · tone: epic war
Logline: Goguryeo spent fourteen years building a wall. The Blue Dragon simply walks around it.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Every wall assumes the enemy will knock. Goguryeo has spent fourteen years building a wall of forts along the river. The Blue Dragon simply walks around it. He shows his banners on the middle road, then turns north in the night. By morning his horse are across an unwatched ford. The first fortress shuts its gates. It holds exactly as long as the gates do.
[1] [MAP 645: Banners on the middle road, horses at the northern ford. Goguryeo watched the banners.]
[2] ¶ The New Fortress doesn’t fall. The emperor’s cousin spends ten days under its walls and leaves with nothing. So the Blue Dragon posts a guard on it and turns south. The next fort lasts a little over ten days. Seven hundred men Yeon sent to hold it are taken in the gate. They ask to serve the emperor instead.
[3] The Second Emperor: Their homes are all in Gasi, I am told. / If they fight for Us, the Mangniji will kill every wife and child they have. / To gain one man’s arm by wiping out his house — that We cannot bring Ourselves to do. Send them home.
[4] ¶ They go home with grain for the road. It is a kindness, and it is also arithmetic: seven hundred men who have seen the size of this army will describe it to Gasi better than any envoy could.
[5] ¶ Between the army and the walls lies the Liao marsh. Two hundred li of mud. A Sui host once went in up to the knee and came out as a song. The emperor’s engineer lays a road of earth across it, wide enough for carts. When the last wagon is over, the emperor has the road torn up. Nobody goes home the way they came. He wants every man in the column to know it.
[6] ¶ Then Yodong itself, the Eastern Fortress. It held off the last dynasty for three summers and never opened. The Blue Dragon has already driven one sortie back through the gate when the emperor arrives. He rides to the moat with a sack of earth across his saddle and throws it in. His officers can’t be seen carrying less than him. They carry two. The army rings the walls a hundred deep and beats the drums until the ground answers.
[7] [PLACE yodong: The gate the West keeps knocking on.]
[8] ── SCENE: The Shrine ──
[9] ¶ Inside the walls there is a shrine to the Holy King. Ask the town who he was and they say Jumong, as if that settles it. A coat of chain mail hangs in it, and a long sharp spear, and the town will tell you both came down from heaven. By the eighth day stones are coming over the parapet. The elders choose a girl from the town, wash her, paint her, dress her in red silk and a bride’s crown, and walk her up to the shrine to be given to the god.
[10] 👰: It’s… heavy. The dress. / …Tell my mum. Tell her I didn’t cry.
[11] 🔔: The Holy King… is smiling. / He has taken his bride! This city will stand whole!
[12] ¶ They close the shrine door on her. The town sleeps better that night. She doesn’t.
[13] ¶ The Holy King isn’t consulted again. The Blue Dragon’s throwers hurl rocks the size of grain jars over the walls. Towers roll up to the parapet. On the twelfth day a south wind rises. They fire the south-west tower, and the wind carries it into town.
[14] ¶ The fire takes the town street by street. The shrine is stone, so it is the last roof standing when the gate gives. A Tang squad kicks its door in, looking for gold.
[15] ¶ They find a girl in red silk sitting under the chain mail, holding the god’s spear the wrong way round.
[16] 👰: Don’t. / I’m married.
[17] ¶ The soldiers laugh. Then the emperor’s horse is in the doorway, and nobody laughs.
[18] The Second Emperor: Whose bride is this?
[19] 🪖: Their god’s, Majesty. The one who owns the armour.
[20] The Second Emperor: Then We do not take another man’s wife. Not even a dead man’s. / Leave her to him. Let the city see what its god can do for her.
[21] ¶ When the fighting stops, the clerks count ten thousand dead, then lose interest and count the grain. The fortress a million men couldn’t open has lasted twelve days.
[22] ¶ Veterans spit and say the real argument is still ahead, at **Ansi**.
[23] ── SCENE: Below Ansi ──
[24] ¶ Then the Second Emperor rides on to look at Ansi, and the man who holds it comes out onto the wall to look back. Nobody on the Tang side ever writes down his name.
[25] [CARD The Guardian: The man who holds Ansi. The other side never learns his name, and he never offers it.]
[26] The Second Emperor: You. On the wall. Your name. / We like to know whom We are about to forgive.
[27] The Guardian: You will simply… have to call me the man on the wall. / I hear you don’t care for names anyway.
[28] The Second Emperor: A nameless man, then. / History will not trouble itself to remember you. We are the one writing it.
[29] The Guardian: Write fast, then. / You’ve got two hundred li of mud behind you and no road home. I’ve got a wall and all autumn.
[30] ¶ The emperor does not ask twice. Nobody has ever made him ask twice. He turns his horse and starts looking at the ground around Ansi the way a cook looks at a goose.
[31] ── SCENE: The Rest of the Line ──
[32] ¶ The rest of the line comes down like roof tiles. At White Cliff, Yeon’s riders break out and put a spear into the White Dragon’s waist. He has it bound and is back in the saddle by evening, laughing.
[33] Lord of White Cliff: He’s back on his horse. With a hole in him. / …Open the gate. I’m not fighting a man who laughs at spears.
[34] ¶ Of all the forts Yeon spent fourteen years hauling stone for, two still fly Goguryeo’s banners. One of them is Ansi.
[35] [MAP 645 The rest of the line: A spear in the White Dragon, a fleet on the cape. The tiles keep falling anyway.]
[36] ── SCENE: Pyongyang ──
[37] ¶ In Pyongyang, Gesomun reads the Yodong report twice and feeds it to the brazier.
[38] Yeon Gesomun: Twelve days. / The Sui sat outside that wall for three summers. This one does it in twelve days! / Go Yeonsu. How many can you march by the new moon?
[39] Go Yeonsu: A hundred and fifty thousand, Supreme Commander. With the Mohe horse.
[40] Yeon Gesomun: Good. Go to Ansi. Meet him in the open and break him on the plain. / And take my boys with the baggage. Let them watch an emperor run.
[41] ¶ An old officer at the end of the table clears his throat. He has been clearing it for forty years. This time he finishes.
[42] The old officer: The open field, sir? With respect. / The last king who met an empire in the open… didn’t look at the ground.
[43] Yeon Gesomun: Then tell Go Yeonsu on the road. You’ve got four days. Make it short.
[44] ¶ **On the road to Ansi, the old man tells it anyway. Once, a king won twice and went back for a third…!**

=================================================================
#33 Boiling River  (244)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: Part II — The Dawn of War / The Seventh Invasion · place: gungnae · tone: epic war legend
Logline: A king picks a fight over a diplomatic spat. Then he picks a battlefield he hasn’t looked at.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ The old officer starts with the part kings like to hear. Goguryeo won. Twice.
[1] [CARD King Dongcheon: A king who starts a war over a letter. This time, someone writes back.]
[2] [MAP 244: ]
[3] ¶ Four hundred years back, King Dongcheon picked a fight with the northern empire of Wei. Wei sent its most famous general to explain why that was a mistake. Goguryeo met him at the Boiling River and won. Then it won again.
[4] King Dongcheon: Wei’s great army is worse than our small one. / Their famous general? His life is in the palm of my hand. / Five thousand horse. We ride now.
[5] The captain: Majesty, the ground past the river— nobody’s ridden it. / Let me send scouts. One afternoon.
[6] King Dongcheon: One afternoon is all I need to win.
[7] ¶ So the king took five thousand horse out to win a third time, on ground he had not looked at. The Wei general formed a square on a slope that ran his way. The square held. The horses didn’t. Eighteen thousand men died in an afternoon.
[8] King Dongcheon: …I did not look at the ground.
[9] ¶ Hwando is burned. The king runs east with a handful of men, and the Wei riders are one valley behind and closing.
[10] ¶ At a ford in the rain, the captain who asked for scouts holds out his hand.
[11] The captain: Your robe, Majesty. / They’re chasing a king’s robe. Let them catch one.
[12] King Dongcheon: …Your name. I never even asked your name.
[13] The captain: You didn’t look at the ground either, Majesty. / Go.
[14] ¶ He rides back up the valley in the king’s robe, slowly, so they can see it. They see it. Nobody on either side writes down his name.
[15] [PLACE hwando: A mountain capital, built for the day the plain is lost.]
[16] ¶ Goguryeo takes forty years to be a kingdom again. It is the first time in this story that a Samhan capital burns because of one bad afternoon, and it is not the last, and every king in this record has heard about it.
[17] ¶ On the road to Ansi, the young general hears him out politely, the way you let a grandfather finish.
[18] Go Yeonsu: Good story, grandfather. / But he had five thousand horse. I have a hundred and fifty thousand men.
[19] The old officer: …So did Wei.
[20] ¶ **A hundred and fifty thousand men march toward an open plain. On a hill above it, the emperor is waiting…!**

=================================================================
#34 Stallion Mountain  (645 June)
Arc: Part II — The Dawn of War / The Seventh Invasion · place: jupil · tone: epic war — clash of heroes
Logline: A farmer in a white coat walks onto the field as a name on a muster roll. The Emperor is watching.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Go Yeonsu liked the old man’s story. He just didn’t think it was about him.
[1] [PLACE jupil: Named for where an emperor stopped. Emperors name a lot of things.]
[2] [MAP 645: Goguryeo sends a hundred and fifty thousand down the crow road. The emperor sends himself.]
[3] ¶ At Stallion Mountain the Second Emperor does not wait behind the line.
[4] The Second Emperor: I myself am the **vanguard**…!
[5] ¶ The relief army comes down the crow road under banners that think numbers are an argument. **Go Yeonsu** and **Go Hyejin** ride at the front. Across the plain, under a hill, the Tang look like a single army of fifteen thousand.
[6] The old officer: That isn’t all of them. / An emperor doesn’t come this far with fifteen thousand. Dig in. Cut his grain. Let winter do the fighting.
[7] Go Yeonsu: Winter isn’t here, grandfather. He is. In person. / We will never get a better chance at an emperor’s head.
[8] ¶ Nobody tells Go Yeonsu about the valley behind him. A second army has gone round through it in the night, with the Black Dragon at its head.
[9] ¶ At dawn, drums start on the mountain above the field. The emperor is up there with his horns and his flags, playing the battle like a court orchestra.
[10] ── SCENE: The Tang Line ──
[11] ¶ In the Tang line stands a guard captain whose accent still has the sea in it. Sul Gedu left Silla twenty-four winters ago, in the hold of a merchant ship. When the emperor called for volunteers, he put his own name down. It’s the only way a foreigner gets a captain’s sash. Across the field, the enemy’s banners are close enough to read.
[12] 🪖: Hey, Captain Xue. That lot over there… they say they’re Samhan men. / Aren’t you from Samhan as well?
[13] Sul Gedu: Samhan. Silla. / In Silla they count your bones before they hire you. Doesn’t matter how big your talent is or how big your deeds — wrong bones, and you don’t get over the wall. You just don’t. / So I crossed the sea. To walk in and out at the Son of Heaven’s side with a cap and a sash and a sword. / …That’ll do me.
[14] ¶ The soldier laughs, not sure he was meant to. Sul Gedu ties off his helmet cord and does not look at the banners again.
[15] ¶ In the Tang line a low officer decides the field needs a mark it cannot look away from. He puts on **white armour** — not for mourning, for visibility — hangs two bows at his waist, takes up the **fangtian ji**, and rides into the front so hard the relief army has to notice him or die without knowing why.
[16] Xue Rengui: Make a path. / If you will not — the ji will.
[17] ¶ No one in the Goguryeo line stops him for long. Then the drums on the mountain change, and the Black Dragon’s banners come out of the valley behind them. The relief army turns to face the wrong way twice. The formation breaks. The mountain learns a new colour.
[18] ❝QUOTE (Zizhi Tongjian (資治通鑑) bk. 198, Tang Zhenguan 19 (645), 6th month): Just then came thunder and lightning. Xue Rengui, a man of Longmen, in strange clothing, broke into the enemy line with a great shout, and nothing could stand before him. The Goguryeo troops gave way; the main army followed through, and the Goguryeo troops broke completely…❞
[19] The Second Emperor: Who is that man in white armour. / The one at the tip of the spear.
[20] Blue Dragon: Xue Rengui, Your Majesty. / A soldier… who was a farmer.
[21] ¶ They bring him up. Dirt on the white. Blood on the crescent of the ji. He kneels like a man who has never been in a palace and does not intend to apologise for it.
[22] The Second Emperor: My old generals are all aged. / I have been looking for a fierce one to entrust the frontier to — and I find none better than you. / I am less happy about gaining Liaodong than about gaining you.
[23] Xue Rengui: A farmer… how could he dare. / This ji only widened Your Majesty’s road a little.
[24] ¶ They give him gold, silk, a general’s title, and a place among the men who stand at the northern gate. The white coat stays. So does the ji.
[25] ¶ That night he has a clerk write home for him. Two lines. The mounds can be finished properly now. Liu should buy the good stone.
[26] ¶ Go Yeonsu pulls what is left onto a hill to regroup. Behind the hill, the Tang have already burned the bridges. Nobody goes home the way they came. The emperor likes that trick.
[27] ¶ When the dust settles, the two relief commanders walk into the Tang camp and surrender. Thirty-six thousand men walk in behind them. The officers are sent inland, to be subjects far from any border. The common soldiers are sent home. The three thousand Mohe riders who came south with them are marched into a valley and buried alive.
[28] ¶ Go Yeonsu does not live out the year. The records say he died of grief, which is the only cause of death the Tang ever let a surrendered general keep.
[29] ── SCENE: The Field at Night ──
[30] ¶ There is another foreigner in the reckoning that night. Riding over the ground where the Goguryeo centre stood, the emperor finds Sul Gedu farther in than any of his own men got, face down among the dead he made.
[31] The Second Emperor: Who is this? / He is further in than any of Ours.
[32] Blue Dragon: A Silla man, Majesty. Sul Gedu. / His friends say he wanted a cap, a sash and a sword. At your side.
[33] The Second Emperor: Our own men look about them and will not advance. A foreigner dies for Us. / Give him the rank. Bury him with full rites.
[34] ¶ Then he takes off the imperial robe and lays it over the dead man himself.
[35] ¶ The cap, the sash and the sword, more or less. He gets them lying down.
[36] ¶ Fame is a short leash. Before the army even settles into the Ansi siege, Goguryeo stops trying to kill the man in white in the open and starts trying to keep him.
[37] ── SCENE: The Cell Under the Wall ──
[38] ¶ They take him in a night fight east of the Liao — nets, numbers, the ji knocked from his hands — and drag him inland to a lesser fortress that is not Ansi and does not want to be famous. Iron on the wrists. A cell under the wall. The white coat cut off him like a trophy.
[39] Gate Guard: The Second Emperor… is coming this way. / Tonight. With silver, to buy back the man in white. Holy King, look down.
[40] Xue Rengui: …Before His Majesty arrives. / I will have to be out.
[41] ¶ He breaks the irons. He breaks the door. The white coat only made him easy to see.
[42] ¶ He finds the ji on a rack in the yard, still sticky from someone else’s hands, and takes the wall the way water takes a crack. By the time the Second Emperor’s banners show on the ridge, the cell is empty and the fortress is explaining itself to no one.
[43] The Second Emperor: …That white coat again. / Arriving before Us, I see.
[44] Xue Rengui: I could not keep Your Majesty waiting. / The chains… were impolite.
[45] ¶ The Second Emperor laughs once — short, relieved — and does not ask how. A sovereign who has to ask how has already lost the man.
[46] ── SCENE: Two Boys ──
[47] ¶ Among the prisoners taken at the mountain are two boys, eleven and eight: Gesomun’s sons, the careful one and the one who never backs down first. Their father sent them with the baggage to watch an emperor run.
[48] The Second Emperor: So. Gai Suwen’s sons. / Your father killed his king. I killed my brothers. / So you see, he and I understand one another.
[49] The Second Emperor: Here is my offer. / Kneel, call yourselves servants of the Great Tang, and I will give you both titles. / A house in Chang’an, silk, a name. Things Goryeo will never give you.
[50] Yeon Namgun: Brother.
[51] ¶ Namseng is eleven. He works out, quite quickly, that the Second Emperor wants two and will settle for one, and that only one of them has to be the one who refuses.
[52] Yeon Namseng: Your Majesty. My brother is small. He understands nothing. / It is I who refuse. Give the punishment to me.
[53] The Second Emperor: …You are the elder?
[54] Yeon Namseng: I am.
[55] ¶ They flog him in front of his brother and send them both back across the Liao in the spring, as a gesture. Namgun does not speak for the whole journey.
[56] Yeon Namgun: You took it for me.
[57] Yeon Namseng: I am the elder.
[58] ── SCENE: Pyongyang ──
[59] ¶ The news reaches Pyongyang in two pieces. The field army is gone. The boys are in the emperor’s tent.
[60] Yeon Gesomun: Both of them?
[61] Rider: Both, Supreme Commander. The emperor sends word he will be kind to them.
[62] Yeon Gesomun: Kind. / A man who killed his brothers is being kind to my sons.
[63] ¶ The hall waits for him to break something. He doesn’t. He calls for a map and puts his thumb on the one fort still flying the old king’s colours. The fort that refused him.
[64] Yeon Gesomun: Ansi. That madman. / When I was seven, my father came home from the Colossal River with a Sui flag under his arm. I thought flags grew on emperors. / Let him come deep. The last one did.
[65] ¶ **Why isn’t Gesomun afraid? Go back thirty-three years, to a general who surrendered seven times and won…!**

#35 Colossal River  (612)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: Part II — The Dawn of War / The Seventh Invasion · place: salsu · tone: epic war legend
Logline: Ulchi Munduk surrenders seven times on the way south. Every time, the river gets closer.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Ulchi Munduk surrenders seven times on the way south. Every time, the river gets closer.
[1] [MAP 612: Nine armies over the Liao, a fleet up the Taedong. The Sui planned everything except the walk home.]
[2] ¶ Gesomun is seven that summer. The last dynasty’s emperor has sent three hundred thousand men at Pyongyang. Goguryeo sends one man to look at them.
[3] [PLACE salsu: Ask a Goguryeo grandfather. He will raise a cup first.]
[4] ── SCENE: The Sui Camp ──
[5] ¶ Munduk walks into the enemy camp himself first, to look at them. He brings a white flag, a polite face and no guards. He has come, he says, to surrender.
[6] Sui general: Goguryeo surrenders? Just like that?
[7] Ulchi Munduk: Just like that, General. / We are a small country. You are a very large army. / …How long have your men carried their own rice? They look tired.
[8] ¶ A hundred days of rice each, on their own backs. At night most of them bury half of it under the tent to lighten the load. Munduk notices the fresh dirt.
[9] Sui general: The emperor’s orders are to seize you if you come.
[10] Sui officer: General— if we seize an envoy who came to surrender, nobody will ever surrender to us again.
[11] ¶ So they let him walk out. He has seen everything he came for. By evening the general regrets it and sends a rider after him: come back, there is more to discuss.
[12] Ulchi Munduk: Tell the general I’m flattered. / Tell him we can discuss it further south.
[13] ── SCENE: Seven ──
[14] ¶ He surrenders seven times on the way south and runs seven times. Each time the Sui win a small fight, plant a flag and feel wonderful. Each running pulls them further from their buried rice and closer to Pyongyang.
[15] Sui general: Seven victories in a day! Write that down.
[16] Sui officer: General… we have won seven times and taken nothing. Not one granary.
[17] [MAP 612 The walk home: They marched to within thirty li of Pyongyang. Munduk had been counting on exactly that.]
[18] ¶ Thirty li from Pyongyang, the army stops and looks at the walls. The walls look back. Then a letter arrives from Munduk. It is a poem.
[19] [POEM Poem sent to the Sui general [Ulchi Munduk] (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 44, Biographies — Eulji Mundeok): Your godlike strategy has searched out the patterns of heaven; / your wondrous reckoning has mastered the lie of the land. / Your victories have already won you high merit — / know it is enough, and I pray you stop.]
[20] Sui general: Is he… praising me?
[21] Sui officer: He’s telling you to go home, General.
[22] ¶ A second note follows, plainer. If the Sui turn around, the king of Goguryeo will come and bow to their emperor in person. It is the eighth surrender. The general takes it, because it is the only one he can carry home.
[23] ── SCENE: The River ──
[24] ¶ They turn for home starving. At the Colossal River the water is low and wide, and the army starts across.
[25] Ulchi Munduk: Wait. / …Wait. / Now. While their feet are wet.
[26] ¶ When the army is halfway over, Goguryeo comes down on the rearguard. Men on the far bank can’t come back. Men on the near bank can’t get over. The ones in the middle find out how deep a shallow river is.
[27] ❝QUOTE (Zizhi Tongjian (資治通鑑) bk. 181, Sui Daye 8 (612), 7th month): When the nine armies crossed the Liao there were three hundred and five thousand of them. When they got back to the Liaodong fortress there were two thousand seven hundred. Stores and weapons by the tens of thousands were lost, every one.❞
[28] ¶ Munduk is honored with the title _**“The Defender”**_ after the battle.
[29] ¶ Gesomun’s father rides home through the Pyongyang gate with a Sui banner rolled under his arm like a bolt of cloth. The boy at the gate decides, then and there, what emperors are for.
[30] The boy: Is that the emperor’s?
[31] His father: One of them. Emperors have plenty. / They drop them when they run. Here. Hold it by the pole, not the silk.
[32] ¶ **Yodong fell. The forts fell. One wall is left, held by a madman whose name nobody wrote down…!**

#36 Ansi  (645 September)
Arc: Part II — The Dawn of War / The Seventh Invasion · place: ansi · tone: epic war — the siege
Logline: The Guardian of Ansi refused Yeon to his face. Now the Emperor of the West is at his gate.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ The Guardian of Ansi Fortress is an eccentric man. When Yeon took the country, the Guardian refused him to his face. He kept the old king’s colours on the wall. Yeon had drowned a whole court for less. He looked at that wall, weighed the siege, and rode away. Ansi answers to no one.
[1] [PLACE ansi: One small fortress, and one stubborn man on top of it.]
[2] ¶ Nobody writes his name down. To the people inside the walls he is just the chief, and that turns out to be enough.
[3] [MAP 645: The emperor wants Pyongyang. One small fortress is in the way.]
[4] ▼ FLASHBACK 642 Yeon at Ansi
    [4.0] Yeon Gesomun: Ansi… so that man is still alive. / He dares refuse the Supreme Commander’s order?
    [4.1] The Guardian: I have heard that a true man needs only / one person to cherish, / and one person to serve, / and that is enough.
[4] ▲ end flashback
[5] ── SCENE: The Earthen Mountain ──
[6] ¶ The Second Emperor tries the wall first. When the wall does not work he tries the ground, which is the sort of thing only an empire can afford to try. Goguryeo archers watch him do it from the parapet.
[7] Tang hauler: How many baskets is that now?
[8] Another hauler: Don’t count. It gets heavier when you count.
[9] Ansi soldier: Chief, that’s sixty days they’ve been at it.
[10] The Guardian: Then it’s sixty nights for us. Pass the stone.
[11] ¶ Inside the walls the stone runs out first. Then the doors. Then the roof beams of the houses nearest the south wall. Families sleep in the open and pass their own lintels up the ladder.
[12] ¶ Five hundred thousand man-days, sixty days of hauling, and a mountain of packed earth rises outside the south wall until its crown looks down into the fortress. From up there you can count the cook fires.
[13] [FORMATION Ansi Fortress, sixth to ninth month, 645: Every night the defenders built their wall higher than the mound had grown that day. The siege became a race between shovels.]
[14] ¶ Then it rains, and the mountain slumps — sideways, into the wall it was built to overlook, taking a stretch of Ansi down with it. Both sides stare at the gap.
[15] Ansi soldier: Chief, the wall—
[16] The Guardian: Never mind the wall. Who’s up on that thing right now?
[17] ¶ The officer who was supposed to be holding the mound has stepped away.
[18] Ansi soldier: …There’s nobody up there.
[19] The Guardian: Then it’s ours.
[20] ¶ A few hundred men come out through the gap, take the mountain, pile timber on its slope and set it alight. The Tang cannot get near it for three days.
[21] ¶ The Second Emperor has Fu Fuai, the officer who left the mound, beheaded, and orders three days of assault.
[22] ¶ The emperor rides up to watch. Too close.
[23] ¶ On the second day the Guardian sees him: a yellow parasol on the near slope, closer than any emperor should be. He takes the bow from the archer beside him.
[24] The Guardian: Hold still, you.
[25] ¶ The arrow takes the helmet clean off. The lacquered bowl leaves his head and rings once on packed earth, then keeps rolling. For the first time in the siege, the two men look straight at each other.
[26] The Second Emperor: …That man. / Find out his name.
[27] ¶ Nobody can. A cut over the emperor’s eye bleeds into his beard. The surgeons say it is nothing, and he lets them.
[28] ── SCENE: The Retreat ──
[29] ¶ Then the cold comes early. Sixty days of hauling earth were sixty days of horses eating the plain, and the plain is bare. There is nothing left to feed them.
[30] ¶ On the morning he turns for home, the emperor parades his army under the wall one last time, so the wall can see what it beat. Inside, nobody shows a face. Then one man climbs the parapet and bows.
[31] ¶ A proper bow, from the waist. The kind you give a guest who stayed too long.
[32] The Second Emperor: Bring up the silk. A hundred bolts. / For a man who serves his lord well. Let every wall in Our empire hear of it. / And ask him his name. Once more.
[33] The Guardian: Tell him thanks for the silk. / And tell him this. You may outnumber us. You may outthink us. / But you will never be crazier than we are…!
[34] ¶ The silk goes up the wall on a rope. The name does not come down.
[35] ¶ Then the marsh. Two hundred li of mud, and the road across it is the road he tore up himself. Nobody goes home the way they came. He said that.
[36] ¶ Snow comes down on the column in the mud. The emperor gets off his horse and cuts brush with his own hands to fill the ruts. His officers can’t be seen carrying less.
[37] The Second Emperor: With all the armies under heaven, how was I humiliated by so small a barbarian land? / …If the old minister were alive, he would never have let me come. / Somebody tell me no. Anybody.
[38] ¶ Nobody does. That was the whole trouble.
[39] [MAP 645 The Seventh Invasion, start to finish: All those arrows in, and two dotted lines out. One small wall did that.]
[40] ── SCENE: The Gate ──
[41] ¶ Three weeks later a rider in red comes up the empty road from Pyongyang, alone. The last time he came, he looked at this wall and rode away.
[42] The Guardian: Supreme Commander! Come for my head, now the work’s done?
[43] Yeon Gesomun: Madman… / Still — you did what had to be done.
[44] Yeon Gesomun: Keep your head. Keep your old colours. Keep your gate shut, I don’t care. / I came to see what stopped him. It’s smaller than I thought.
[45] The Guardian: So’s the emperor, up close.
[46] ¶ Gesomun laughs, a laugh like a slap, and turns his horse. He does not ask to come in. The Guardian does not offer.
[47] ── SCENE: Yodong ──
[48] ¶ He rides home by way of Yodong. The Tang marched its people west when they left, seventy thousand of them, roped in lines. What is left is ash, and a stone shrine on the hill with its door open.
[49] ¶ Under the chain mail sits a girl in red silk gone the colour of rust. A lamp beside her. She has kept it lit for three months on what the soldiers left behind.
[50] 👰: You’re not him either.
[51] Yeon Gesomun: Who?
[52] 👰: My husband. Everybody else went west. The emperor said I belonged to him, so they left me here. / …Nobody ever told me who he is. They just gave me to him.
[53] Yeon Gesomun: Nobody told you. / …Ha. Move over. It’s a long one. It starts with a god looking down at a girl in a river.
[54] ¶ **Who was the Holy King, and why does Goguryeo give him brides? Seven hundred years back, the sun looked down…!**

#37 Haemosu  (-37)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: Part II — The Dawn of War / The Seventh Invasion · place: buyeo_north · tone: founder fairy tale
Logline: Every day the sun crosses the sky on the same road. Today he looks down.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Every day the sun crosses the sky on the same road. Today he looks down.
[1] ¶ The sky is empty first. Then come five dragons in the yoke, gold, crimson, azure, jade and white, and behind them a small gold chariot cutting the noon on the run they make every day. From the ground it is a fleck and a wheel, nothing a bather could call a face. The driver stands in it the way a man stands in a doorway he owns, one palm on the rail, laughing at nothing in particular.
[2] [MAP -37: ]
[3] ¶ Dawn, noon, dusk, night, always the same route. Below, the Amnok is a line he is not supposed to break: wet stone, morning shallows with no boat in them, rocks that are only rocks.
[4] [PLACE amnok: Every god’s road crosses it. Most of them keep going.]
[5] ¶ **Haemosu**, god of the sun, has kept this hour since before the river had daughters. Today the Amnok flashes under the wheel. He looks down, and the hour breaks.
[6] [CARD Haemosu: The sun god. Punctual since before the rivers, until this afternoon.]
[7] ¶ In the shallows, three river-daughters are bathing: Yuhwa and her two sisters. Wet hair down their backs, the river at their hips. Nobody dressed for heaven. He falls in love and in lust in the same glance.
[8] [CARD Lady Yuhwa: The river’s youngest daughter, a nymph of the Amnok. Heaven is about to ruin her afternoon, or make it.]
[9] [CARD Hwahye: The eldest river-daughter. First into the water, every time.]
[10] [CARD Wihye: The middle sister. She laughs first and dives second.]
[11] ¶ Hwahye and Wihye have left their silk on the rocks. The eldest folded hers once; the middle did not bother. Yuhwa’s ice-blue is still on her shoulder, wet.
[12] ¶ Yuhwa kneels in the shallows with her hair in one fist like a dark rope and rinses the river out of it without hurrying. Heaven can wait on a rinse; she has decided that without saying it. With her back to the sky she looks over her shoulder, as if someone up there had said her name.
[13] Haemosu: …Stop. Stop the chariot.
[14] Haemosu: Those thighs… / The water…
[15] Lady Yuhwa: Unni. / Go. I’m here. / …I was going to say don’t look up.
[16] Hwahye: Hey. In. / Now. You hear me?
[17] ¶ Hwahye dives first and does not look back. The eldest treats the sky like a timetable she will not miss.
[18] Wihye: Pfft— wait up. / You, seriously— / Whatever, I’m going—
[19] ¶ Wihye laughs and follows, a splash that is mostly amusement.
[20] ¶ Two wakes cut the shallows and close. Yuhwa stays. She gets up off her knees, looks straight up as if she had been waiting for heaven to notice, and draws her wet hair over one shoulder.
[21] ¶ She draws the wet silk higher, one hip and then the other, and lets the sun finish looking.
[22] Haemosu: Hey— / Wait. Hey. You. / Why aren’t you hiding? Look at me like that and I’m coming down.
[23] Lady Yuhwa: Heaven looks down every day. / So today I’m supposed to blush? / …Come closer, if you want to see. / Into the water. / And decide… where your hands are going.
[24] Haemosu: …Your name. / I need it… before I come down. / Or… I kiss you without one.
[25] Lady Yuhwa: Come down first. / From the sky it’s an order. / At the water… I’ll hear it as a request. / Ask with your mouth… and I’ll answer with my name.
[26] ¶ He forgets how to swallow, a god doing a mortal’s small panic. Then he grins, and the grin arrives before the plan. He leaves the rail and the hour in the same motion, the dragons keep the joke going without him, and the water takes him at the knee.
[27] ¶ He wades close. She does not run. He stops where a stranger should stop. Then he doesn’t.
[28] Haemosu: Why didn’t you run away? / Your sisters did.
[29] Lady Yuhwa: …Didn’t see any reason. / The water’s cold. You’re warm. That’s all there is to it.
[30] Haemosu: Look straight at the sun / and you burn.
[31] Lady Yuhwa: Oh, is that so? / Then I should blink.
[32] Haemosu: It’ll burn your eyes out. / I’m not a lamp.
[33] Lady Yuhwa: I like what I see. / I’m looking anyway. You came down. / Don’t make me say it twice.
[34] ¶ He swallows. The grin survives it. Barely.
[35] ¶ She tips her mouth and asks whether the sun likes what it sees, silk already losing the argument with the water.
[36] Lady Yuhwa: This way. The bank. / The sky has too many sisters.
[37] ¶ He follows like the hour had been her idea.
[38] ¶ The copper room rises on the bank like a kiln. He builds it the same afternoon, because the open sky has become too many witnesses.
[39] Lady Yuhwa: Copper gets hot in summer. / …You’ll know if you touch it. / My back, too. / If you press me to it… you won’t tell which burned you.
[40] Haemosu: I know. / That’s why I can’t take my hands off you. / Or my mouth.
[41] Lady Yuhwa: Then don’t. / Not while heaven is watching.
[42] Lady Yuhwa: And while it watches… deeper.
[43] ¶ She kisses him with river still on her mouth. The kiss tastes like the shallows. He makes a sound he will deny.
[44] ¶ Inside, the copper has kept the afternoon’s heat. She leans into it and does not look away from him. Gold lies across wet skin in a hard bar, and the ice-blue silk slips from one shoulder, then gives up the other.
[45] Lady Yuhwa: If you want it, say so. / I’m not asking twice.
[46] Lady Yuhwa: Give me— all of it. / Don’t save any.
[47] ¶ He puts her back to it anyway. The river-silk is gathered at her hip and her thighs close around a sun-god who has never learned to be gentle with an hour. She takes him in with the same wet hand that washed her hair for heaven, and when he is all the way inside her she laughs, as if this were what she had meant by looking.
[48] Lady Yuhwa: Haa— is heaven always this heavy? / More— against the copper— don’t stop—
[49] Haemosu: I broke the hour. / I don’t care. / Your name— now—
[50] Lady Yuhwa: Yuhwa— ah— it’s Yuhwa— / Stay— stay inside me— / All of it— the whole sun—
[51] ¶ He takes her through the heat of the wall, gold on wet skin, and every stroke knocks a sound out of her that the river throws back. She comes first and loudly, looking up as if heaven were still watching. Then he spills into her, a god’s whole careless heat, and does not draw back, because she told him not to, and because the hour is already ruined.
[52] ¶ The copper keeps the afternoon. Outside, the river goes on being a river.
[53] ¶ Up on the road, the dragons have hauled an empty chariot to dusk on their own. Half the world got its evening late. Heaven noticed.
[54] Haemosu: They’re calling. / I’m late. I’m never late.
[55] Lady Yuhwa: Go, then. / …Come back tomorrow. Same hour. I’ll break it for you this time.
[56] Haemosu: They won’t let me come down twice. Not while I’m up there. / Hey. Don’t look at me like that. I’ll find a way.
[57] ¶ He goes up in a flash of copper. Heaven fines the sun the only way it can: while he is in the sky, he may not set foot on the earth. He may look. He may talk. That is all.
[58] ── SCENE: Habek's Court ──
[59] ¶ The copper is still warm when the river notices. The Amnok keeps its own court: **Habek**, god of the river and father of three daughters, stands on the wet stones as if the current were a hall. Mist is the dais. He does not need a chair.
[60] [CARD Habek: The Amnok’s river god. He keeps his borders the way kings do, and his daughters the same way.]
[61] Habek: Who stopped the chariot. Say a name.
[62] Lady Yuhwa: I… looked up. / I just— looked. That’s all it was.
[63] Habek: You don’t sleep in my mist after that. / You smell like copper.
[64] Habek: Go. The bank is closed.
[65] ¶ Hwahye and Wihye do not argue the sentence. The eldest watches the current. The middle one watches the copper glow die. Neither looks at their father’s face.
[66] ¶ Habek kicks Yuhwa out with a look, not a foot. The bank understands.
[67] ¶ The pavilion walkway does not catch her. Habek’s sleeve is already the closed door. She hits packed earth with ice-blue still wet from the copper.
[68] ¶ For a while nobody comes. The mist that used to be a bed is just weather. She sits where the river can see her and does not look up.
[69] ¶ The sky talks first. She hears him before she sees anything with paws.
[70] Haemosu: Hey. / Wait. Don’t sit in the dust. / Follow the fox.
[71] ¶ The fox is already on the packed earth, pale gold-white, looking back once as if she might miss the joke. Yuhwa follows it south, barefoot, the ice-blue gone dull with dust: pine shade, a river-bend that is not the Amnok, a pass of bare stone where she is smaller than the ridge. The fox does not explain the map.
[72] ── SCENE: Buyeo ──
[73] ¶ From the river, Buyeo’s capital is a palisade of timber teeth and a hill of grey roofs. The studded doors open. King Geumwa, the gold-frog king, comes out to the yard himself.
[74] [CARD King Geumwa: The gold-frog king. Found under a rock, raised in a palace, kind to strays.]
[75] [PLACE buyeo_north: An old kingdom that takes in strays and keeps count.]
[76] King Geumwa: Come in. I’ve got a room free. / The yard can learn your name later.
[77] ¶ A sun-shaft finds her where she kneels to wring the river out of her sleeve. When she crosses the yard at night it moves with her, a bar of gold keeping her sleeve.
[78] ¶ Yuhwa’s ice-blue sleeve is the first roof the boy will remember, though he is not a boy yet.
[79] ¶ In time Yuhwa lays a great egg. Geumwa has the egg taken from her before the court has agreed what a river-daughter is allowed to bear.
[80] ¶ **Dogs won't eat it. An axe won't split it. What on earth is inside Yuhwa's egg…?**

#38 Buyeo  (-37)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: Part II — The Dawn of War / The Seventh Invasion · place: buyeo_north · tone: founder fairy tale
Logline: Dogs won’t eat it. Hooves step around it. An axe won’t split it. Nobody in the hall wants to say what it is.
=================================================================
[0] ── SCENE: The Egg ──
[1] ¶ Buyeo tries very hard to get rid of the egg. The egg declines.
[2] ¶ Dogs and pigs will not eat it; the sty refuses the guest, and the ministers pretend that is a kind of answer. In the road, cattle and horses step around it, hooves knowing better than the hall. In the open field, birds cover it with their wings instead of pecking, and the yard goes quiet at that.
[3] [MAP -37: ]
[4] ¶ An axe is brought. The axe will not split the egg. The edge sings and the shell does not bother to crack.
[5] ¶ Someone winds up with both arms and hurls it off the palisade. It meets the stones and stays whole.
[6] ¶ Yuhwa wraps it warm in her own sleeve and takes it back upstairs, and nobody reaches for the axe again.
[7] ¶ Then the shell gives, and out comes a baby boy, wet and furious, already trying to focus. He looks up as if the room had owed him an explanation.
[8] ¶ They name him **Jumong**, the good shot, because in those days people were named for what heaven had plainly already decided. He grows up with Geumwa’s sons, Daeso and Galsa.
[9] ¶ They are boys first, three princes at one stake in one square, before anybody is an heir on purpose. They shoot with borrowed bows, too long in the arm.
[10] ¶ Jumong can find a fly’s wing with an arrow before the bow fits his arm.
[11] [CARD Jumong: The best archer in Buyeo. The princes have noticed.]
[12] Jumong: I’ll take the fly.
[13] ¶ Daeso teaches the grip, then resents the hit. The lesson ends the moment the arrow is better than the teacher.
[14] ¶ The yard hears the wood take it, a clean tick, and the praise does not arrive. Daeso keeps his hands on his own bow as if applause were a confession. Galsa looks at the dirt instead of the hit.
[15] ¶ They sleep in a pile like dogs under one quilt, and in the morning the quilt has taken sides. Jumong steals the last millet and grins through it, which is worse than the theft.
[16] ¶ Yuhwa watches from the hall door, ice-blue sleeve on the post, not stepping into the boys’ weather.
[17] ¶ Only two come back talking from the stake. The third has already started a country in his head.
[18] ── SCENE: The Mark-Stake ──
[19] ¶ Grown, they still shoot at the princes’ mark-stake. Daeso stands too close when Jumong’s arrow lands.
[20] [CARD Daeso: Buyeo’s crown prince. Good with a bow, until someone is better.]
[21] Daeso: Do not outshoot the house that feeds you.
[22] Jumong: Then put the mark farther.
[23] [CARD Galsa: Geumwa’s younger son. He smiles at everything, for now.]
[24] Galsa: If it lands, I meant to applaud.
[25] ¶ Jumong keeps the grin because grinning is cheaper than asking why, and Daeso hates the price.
[26] ¶ Jumong’s arranged marriage to Lady Ye is a hall’s solution: a wife, a lamp, a door that still opens onto Buyeo.
[27] [WEDDING Jumong + Lady Ye]
[28] ¶ Lady Ye gets pregnant with their son Yuri while the yard is still pretending the foundling is a guest.
[29] ── SCENE: The Side Room ──
[30] ¶ Geumwa will not take the heir’s counsel, so Daeso takes the ministers into a side room. Lamp low. If they write it down, the scandal arrives before the knife.
[31] Daeso: Do it before the next hunt. / Quiet is fine.
[32] ¶ **Geumwa** answers his heir the way tired kings answer. He refuses the knife and gives the foundling a chore instead: Jumong is sent to the royal stables, which in Buyeo is where a hall keeps a prince it would rather not see at dinner.
[33] ¶ The stables come with three boys who smell worse than he does. Oi, who is always already packing. Mari, who asks why. Hyupbo, who carries the extra. By the end of the month they are his.
[34] ── SCENE: The Stable ──
[35] ¶ **Yuhwa** comes to the stable after the lamps are out, a river-daughter in a frog-king’s straw, and finds her son brushing the best horse in Buyeo as if he could apologise to it in advance.
[36] Lady Yuhwa: This one, isn’t it? / The fast one.
[37] Jumong: …How’d you know? / I didn’t tell anyone.
[38] Lady Yuhwa: You brush this one longer than the others. / I’ll give you a needle. Put it in his tongue. / Say sorry later, and feed him till he bursts.
[39] Jumong: Mother, you’re terrifying. / …For how many days?
[40] Lady Yuhwa: Until Daeso’s done sharpening.
[41] ¶ By the next moon the fastest horse in the yard looks like a rack of kindling with a mane, and the slow ones shine like lacquer. Geumwa walks the stalls, picks the fattest for himself, and tosses the thin one to the foundling with a joke about how well they match. Daeso laughs loudest, which is a pity, because he is the one man in Buyeo who should have looked twice.
[42] King Geumwa: Suits you. / You both eat my rice and still stay thin.
[43] Jumong: Thank you, Majesty. / I’ll take good care of him.
[44] ¶ He pulls the needle out that night. The horse eats until dawn.
[45] ── SCENE: The Knife ──
[46] ¶ Before the next hunt, a knife comes through the dark of his room. Lady Ye’s lamp is still lit, so the shadow moves on the wall before the man does. Jumong rolls. The blade goes into the quilt up to the hilt.
[47] ¶ The man runs. He wears a palace sleeve, and he runs toward Daeso’s end of the hall.
[48] [CARD Lady Ye: A Buyeo girl with a steady hand and a long memory.]
[49] Lady Ye: Leave Buyeo. Tonight. / I’ll keep the lamp.
[50] ¶ He takes his sword down from the wall and breaks it across the seven-sided stone under the pine pillar. It takes two tries. He is not a swordsman.
[51] Jumong: Half stays. In the crack, under the pillar. / If it’s a boy, tell him: under the pine, on the seven-sided stone. He’ll work it out.
[52] Lady Ye: And if it’s a girl?
[53] Jumong: Then she’ll work it out faster.
[54] Jumong: Leave the door half open. / So I know which way is still yours.
[55] ¶ Night at the palisade. Iron studs, a red sleeve, and a wife who does not come out to wave.
[56] ¶ His friends **Oi**, **Mari** and **Hyupbo** take the hills with him. Behind them come the riders Daeso sent, less a hunt than a net, and under the pines it closes from above.
[57] [MAP -37: Buyeo behind him, Daeso’s riders behind that, and a river ahead with no bridge on it. Yet.]
[58] ── SCENE: The Flight ──
[59] ¶ They split in the pines before the river, four men and one horse between them, the one Geumwa thought was thin.
[60] Oi: We’ll take the ridge. / Find us when you still have a bow.
[61] Jumong: Take him. / Your road over the ridge is longer. I’ll do the river alone.
[62] Oi: Are you crazy? He’s your horse.
[63] Jumong: Exactly. Fatten him up for me. / …I’ll come find you.
[64] ¶ He runs until the pines smear. Behind him the net is spears in the dark, points only, no faces he is allowed to know.
[65] ¶ Something keeps pace with him above the trees, black on black, going from branch to branch without seeming to hurry. A crow. He is too frightened to count its legs.
[66] ¶ Jumong reaches the water alone, his death already written down for that day. No ford. No boat. The friends are a ridge away, on purpose.
[67] ¶ Haewonmek, the reaper who collects each day’s dead, is already in the air. He skims the river toward him. Black hat, black silk, mouth bound shut. Jumong doesn’t see him. He’s looking at the water and the rain.
[68] [CARD Haewonmek: A fetch of the underworld. Black hat, black silk, and a mouth bound shut so he can’t haggle.]
[69] ¶ A root takes his foot. He goes down on the wet stones, pine needles in his mouth, the bow a pace off as if it had been the first thing taken. Haewonmek crouches over him to collect what is owed, and the blow is already coming down.
[70] ¶ The cloak arrives before the face. Rain fills it. A hand closes on Haewonmek’s wrist from behind, and the strike simply stops — the way an elder stops a sleeve that has gone too far.
[71] ¶ Jumong’s cheek is in the mud. Haewonmek looks back. Behind him, in a dark hood, the sun god is holding his wrist and laughing, as if the night had grabbed the wrong man. The night is Haewonmek’s road. The joke is Haemosu’s.
[72] Haewonmek: Haemosu… / The night is not your domain…!
[73] Haemosu: Heh… / Do you really think the sun disappears at night? / I was just crossing the ocean when I heard you coming over.
[74] Haewonmek: This man is fated to die today… / You are not to interfere with Yumla’s domain…!
[75] Haemosu: Hey, Haewonmek. / You’re my little brother and it’s your first week. I’ll go easy on you. / But this is my son. / And he still hasn’t completed his purpose in this world. / And besides… I outrank you. / If Yumla has any complaints, tell him to come see me himself.
[76] ¶ He puts Haewonmek aside and leans to Jumong’s ear. Jumong cannot see him, only the night, the river, a warmth that should not be there. The idea arrives as breath.
[77] ── SCENE: The Crossing ──
[78] Jumong: I am the son of the great Haemosu, the lord of the sun! / Make way for me!
[79] ¶ The river answers. Tortoises rise and lock shell to shell in the dark. Jumong runs the wet backs as if they had always been a road.
[80] ❝QUOTE (Gwanggaeto Stele (廣開土王碑) face I, opening lines (414)): Of old, the founder King Chumo laid the foundations. He came out of North Buyeo, son of the Heavenly Emperor; his mother was Habek’s daughter; he broke the egg and came down into the world… The king came to the ford and said: “I am King Chumo, son of August Heaven, whose mother is Habek’s daughter. Link the reeds and float the turtles for me.” At his voice the reeds linked and the turtles floated, and so he crossed.❞
[81] ¶ The two brothers stay on the near stones. Jumong is already a red speck on the far dark. Haemosu throws an arm across Haewonmek’s shoulder and laughs like the job is done. Haewonmek’s gat is still askew — the look of a clerk whose ledger just walked off.
[82] Haewonmek: He is still mortal…
[83] Haemosu: Yes, of course. / But you know… every man comes into this world for a purpose. / He’s going to do great things. / When his time comes, I’ll let you take him.
[84] Haemosu: Look at him go. / That's my boy.
[85] Haewonmek: You just robbed a ledger.
[86] Haemosu: I borrowed a day. / I'll give it back.
[87] Haewonmek: Yumla isn’t going to like this…
[88] ¶ The bird that watches him is not an ordinary crow. On Goguryeo’s banners it will stand on three legs under a red sun, the **samjoko**, the bird that can look at the day without blinking.
[89] ¶ It is sitting on a rock on the far bank when he comes off the last shell, soaked, laughing like an idiot because he is alive. This time he counts.
[90] Jumong: …One, two. / Three? / Hey. Why’ve you got three legs?
[91] ¶ The crow looks at him without blinking, which is either rude or holy, then drops off the rock, flies ten paces into the pines, lands again, and looks back.
[92] Jumong: Follow you? / …If you’re leading me to a bear, I swear I’m roasting you. / Three legs. There’d be one to spare.
[93] ¶ He follows it all afternoon, uphill, through pines that stop being Buyeo’s and start being nobody’s. It keeps ten paces ahead and never once lets him catch up. At dusk it lands on a stone lip above a dark opening in the hill and stays there, folded, like a doorman whose shift is over.
[94] Jumong: …Here? / Thanks. Really. / Can’t roast you now, can I.
[95] ¶ Before the valley has a name for him he goes in, into stone and leaf-light and a country-shaped dark. In what will be called the Jumong cavern, he prays for a roof of his own.
[96] ¶ **A soaked exile, a hall full of spears, and a chieftain's daughter who won't look at him. Jumong's luck is about to get complicated…!**

#39 Jolbon  (-37)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: Part II — The Dawn of War / The Seventh Invasion · place: jolbon · tone: founder fairy tale
Logline: He’s still wet from the river when the spears find him. The chieftain’s daughter is sharper than the spears.
=================================================================
[0] ── SCENE: The Scouts ──
[1] ¶ He is still wet from the river when the pines stop being empty. Two men in Yeon leather, spears too casual to be hunting, too careful to be lost. Jolbon scouts find him first. The bow is already in the pine needles. His hands are empty and shaking anyway.
[2] [PLACE jolbon: Pine valleys, crow clans, and nobody waiting for a king.]
[3] [MAP -37: From a borrowed stable to a valley of five roofs. The turtles handled the middle part.]
[4] Scout: Stop— stop stop— / Bow—
[5] Second scout: I got him I got— / Red. That’s not ours.
[6] Jumong: Down. It’s down. / Don’t— spear. Please. / Water—
[7] Scout: Hands. Hands where I can see. / You deaf?
[8] Jumong: Yeah. Yeah look. / Just— I ran. River. That’s it.
[9] Second scout: Name. Fast. / If Tabal has to come out here I’m blaming you.
[10] Jumong: Jumong. / Jumong. That’s— that’s the name.
[11] ¶ They bring him in at dusk, not as a guest. One scout keeps looking back like the pines might grow more men. The valley opens under grey giwa. On the porch **Yeon Tabal**, chieftain of Jolbon, holds a cup he is not drinking.
[12] ── SCENE: Tabal’s Hall ──
[13] ¶ Tabal walks him across the packed earth like a man showing a storeroom to a thief: grain porch, well, pine, five roofs that will not share a yard.
[14] [CARD Yeon Tabal: The chief of Jolbon. He shows thieves his storeroom on purpose.]
[15] ¶ Inside, the hall is torches and a man who has not offered a mat. They put Jumong on his knees, packed earth in the weave of his red silk. He tries a grin. It does not survive the torches.
[16] Yeon Tabal: So who sent you.
[17] Jumong: Nobody sent me. / Your men grabbed me. I was just— here.
[18] Yeon Tabal: I asked for a name.
[19] Jumong: Jumong. / That’s the name.
[20] Yeon Tabal: Your clothes don’t look like anything nearby. / Mohe? Khitan? Or the commandery?
[21] ¶ At Tabal’s shoulder stands a woman in dusty-rose silk with a tally-stick in her hand. She has not looked at him once.
[22] Jumong: Pretty. Just—
[23] Yeon Tabal: Eyes. Front.
[24] Sosuno: Count the dirt. / Not him.
[25] Jumong: Ow— I said it.
[26] ¶ Tabal notices the bow. The wood is wrong for every hand in the room except one.
[27] ¶ They put Jumong’s bow in Tabal’s hands. He cannot pull the string, and the limb does not do him the courtesy of bending.
[28] Yeon Tabal: Stop! / Hands off him. / …Whose son are you.
[29] Jumong: Son of Haemosu. / The bow knows. I didn’t ask it to.
[30] ¶ He gives it back, and the wood stays as it was, which is worse than if it had snapped.
[31] Yeon Tabal: Wife?
[32] Jumong: …One. In Buyeo. She told me to run. / So I ran.
[33] ¶ At her father’s shoulder, the woman with the tally-stick makes a small mark she did not need to make.
[34] Yeon Tabal: You're a slave. My daughter's. / Shed. You hunt, you eat. / I do not want ash tracked into my hall.
[35] ¶ For a week Tabal uses him like a tool he has not paid for. West millet has a boar. Two cousins have a ditch and a knife each. Jumong hits both problems and sits in the dirt until someone tells him to stand. Tabal does not thank him. He just stops inventing work.
[36] Yeon Tabal: The millet likes you. I don’t. / Stay anyway. / Shed stays the shed.
[37] Jumong: Yes sir. / …The well’s nicer though.
[38] Yeon Tabal: Then go fetch. Out.
[39] ── SCENE: The Hunt Muster ──
[40] ¶ Tabal’s daughter **Sosuno**, a widow, is already on the grain porch, running Jolbon before she has priced the exile: spear-count, west line, who eats, who rides. The yard answers her first and her father second.
[41] [CARD Sosuno: Tabal’s daughter. She has priced every man in the yard, and she has not finished with this one.]
[42] Sosuno: West line. Two short. / You. Spear. Not that one, the one that isn’t bent. / We leave at first light. If you’re late I leave you.
[43] A hunter: Yes—
[44] Sosuno: Not yes. The count. / East, you’re overlapping. Split. / If I have to say it twice you sit the hunt out.
[45] A hunter: —Split. Sorry.
[46] ¶ Then the wet man is in the yard. Red silk. A back she has not counted. The yard goes quiet. Nobody dropped a spear. They just stopped being loud, because she did.
[47] ¶ Something in her goes stupid while the chin stays up. His father’s name she heard in the hall and filed under nonsense. The line of a shoulder she cannot file anywhere. She will deny all of this to the millet.
[48] Sosuno: …Next. / I said next. / Don’t look at me. Look at the line.
[49] Yeon Tabal: Sosuno. / The line.
[50] Sosuno: I have the line. / West is short two. I said that. / Sun’s in my eyes.
[51] ¶ She starts calling him names because looking is worse. **Big idiot** is the one that sticks. He answers to it on the third day, cheerful, which makes it worse.
[52] ¶ Soon the porch has a name for him too: Sosuno’s worker. She hates how easily it fits.
[53] Sosuno: That’s my worker. / Not yours to stare at.
[54] ¶ One morning she dumps a bucket at his boots and does not bother pretending it slipped. He laughs. Then he says it like it is nothing.
[55] Sosuno: Watch it. / Or don’t. Drown. Whatever.
[56] Jumong: Hey. / You’re pretty when you’re mean. / Like— actually. Sorry. Not sorry.
[57] Sosuno: Ha—!? / Who’s— pretty, what— / It’s not like that!! / Big idiot. Go. Go go—
[58] Jumong: Going. Going. / Sleeve’s wet. Thanks.
[59] ¶ He wrings the sleeve on the way to the shed. She waits until the yard is empty. Then she hides her whole face in the dusty-rose, red to the hairline, whispering idiot at nobody.
[60] ── SCENE: Upstairs ──
[61] ¶ She does not stay in the yard. Chin still up, she takes the loft stairs two at a time like a woman with grain to count. The window faces the millet: his shirt off, red silk knotted at the hip, a back doing work. Whose son he is can wait. The muscles cannot.
[62] ¶ Another afternoon. The dusty-rose is hiked, her thighs apart on the timber, one hand over her mouth and the other talking to the part of her that does not run a hunt: **Little Sosuno**.
[63] Sosuno: Idiot. Don’t grin in my head. / This is your fault, big idiot.
[64] Sosuno: Little Sosuno… you’re hungry today aren’t you… / I don’t blame you…. mmm! look at him… / Those big muscles…. chest…. back…. / Ah fuck dripping wet again… / Out hunting for meat… / I want you to fill me up with some of that meat….
[65] ¶ Tabal is in the doorway of the yard, not the loft, and his voice still climbs the stairs.
[66] Yeon Tabal: Sosuno! / West count. Now. / Don’t make me climb.
[67] ¶ She freezes mid-breath. She smooths the dusty-rose, wipes her hands on her sleeve, and takes the stairs with her chin up. By the packed earth she is the chieftain’s eldest again.
[68] Sosuno: West is short two. / I counted. Twice. / Don’t send the exile. He’ll get lost.
[69] Yeon Tabal: He hit the boar. / You just don’t like his back.
[70] Sosuno: I don’t like his anything. / Can we do the millet.
[71] ── SCENE: Other Daughters ──
[72] ¶ Word gets out that the exile hits what he aims at and looks like a sun when he works shirtless. Jolbon women find reasons to fetch water. Other chieftains mention daughters. Sosuno is suddenly everywhere those reasons are. She finds a flaw every time.
[73] A chieftain: My girl can count. / Strong arms. Good hall.
[74] Sosuno: He walks into buckets. / Can’t wring a sleeve. Talks to millet. / You’d be bored in a week. Big idiot. Next.
[75] ¶ He flirts at the wrong well, which is any well she can see from the porch, and the girls laugh too long at a sentence he did not finish.
[76] Teal: Hey big boy~
[77] Jumong: You’re— yeah. Funny. Too funny.
[78] Teal: Don’t look at Sosuno. Look at me.
[79] Teal: Don’t follow me. / Unless you are.
[80] ¶ Teal hikes her hem at his well like a dare, the rope between them a bad idea, and leans hip first on the beam. The timber takes her weight. His ears take the rest.
[81] ¶ A Sosuno-shaped shadow falls across the rim before her voice does. She is holding an empty bucket she does not need. The girls notice the shadow first, and the laugh dies.
[82] Sosuno: Get. Off. / Get off my well.
[83] Sosuno: This well’s ours. / Ditch is that way. / He doesn’t need help. He needs to work.
[84] Jumong: I was just—
[85] Sosuno: You. Shed. / Don’t smile at them. / Don’t smile at me either.
[86] ¶ He waits until the girls are gone. Then he does not go to the shed. He follows her to the grain post and says it like weather.
[87] Jumong: So. / You keep chasing them off.
[88] Sosuno: BECAUSE YOU WERE HANGING WITH THOSE OTHER BITCHES—
[89] Jumong: The well girls. That chieftain’s kid. You told her I talk to millet.
[90] Sosuno: BECAUSE YOU DO— / WHO ASKED YOU— / I don’t— they’re in the WAY— / This is MY yard— MY well—
[91] Jumong: Okay. Okay. / You’re screaming. / I’m just asking why I can’t say hi.
[92] Sosuno: DON’T HI THEM. / DON’T HI ME. / BIG IDIOT. GET— get off my post—
[93] ¶ She is screaming mad and pink to the hairline and everyone on the porch can hear the hide crack. He grins. That is worse. She leaves him the post. The well she keeps for tomorrow.
[94] ── SCENE: The Well ──
[95] ¶ They keep meeting there as if the rim were a coincidence.
[96] Jumong: Rope’s being a villain. / Want me to—
[97] Sosuno: Pull or don’t. / Talking doesn’t fill it. / Don’t look at my face. / …Sosuno. / There. Now pull.
[98] Jumong: Sosuno. / Cute name. / Your ears are pink.
[99] Sosuno: Wind. / Don’t— look. / You’re so dumb. Pull.
[100] ¶ He keeps ending up thirsty at the same hour. She keeps being there. On the fourth morning he stops pretending the rope is the problem and kisses her at the well-beam.
[101] ¶ She does not pull away first. When she turns, the dusty-rose is wet at the waist from the rope, and she looks back over her shoulder.
[102] Sosuno: You— / How dare you. / My father’s well— / I will kill you. / After. Move.
[103] Jumong: You kissed back. / Just saying.
[104] ¶ He takes the full bucket and actually goes. She stands at the rim until he is a red speck at the shed. Then both hands over her face, furious, shaking.
[105] ¶ She has been collecting him: a thread, a fletch, a length of well-rope, a scrap of his headband, folded into a cloth behind the grain-porch post. He finds it. He holds it up.
[106] Jumong: Hey. / Mice don’t fold headbands. / You hide these like a thief.
[107] ¶ She goes so red the dusty-rose looks pale. She snatches and misses.
[108] Sosuno: Those are— inventory. / Trash. I’ll burn them. / Don’t grin. If you grin I— give it—
[109] Jumong: You’re keeping a little me in a cloth. / Want it back so you can steal it again?
[110] Sosuno: Keep— ha— keep you? / Go get kept somewhere else. Buyeo. Somebody’s keeping a lamp lit for you there, right? A wife with a lamp. / I’m not your— I’m not anybody’s spare bucket.
[111] ¶ He stops smiling. Not angry. Done. He doesn’t lie about the lamp. He has never once lied to her, which is its own kind of problem. He unslings the bow and lays it on packed earth at the well-rim. Then he walks.
[112] Jumong: She told me to run. I ran. / I’m not gonna stay in your yard as something you hide behind a post. / Keep the bow. Tell the millet thanks.
[113] ¶ She does not call stay. She picks the bow up too fast: the bow her father could not bend. She bends it. One arrow. The timber well-beam beside his ear takes it. He stops.
[114] Sosuno: Wait— wait wait— / Don’t. Don’t turn around. / If you look I can’t—
[115] ¶ The confession comes like a tooth she has been biting since the porch. She talks to the dirt, the bow, anything but his mouth.
[116] ¶ The bird pin comes out in her own fingers. Her hair falls in a sheet, and she sits in the dirt with the bow by her knee and talks into the ground, because his face is a luxury she has not paid for.
[117] Sosuno: I don’t— I don’t like you.
[118] Jumong: Then I’m going.
[119] ¶ Then he grins, smaller than the yard grin, asking.
[120] Sosuno: I wasn’t going to say it. / I was gonna let you leave. Stupid. Fine. / Then you put the bow down and I— / I want you. There. Stay. / Don’t make me— I can’t twice. / Big idiot. Other ear. I swear.
[121] Jumong: Hey. Hey I’m here. / Look. Still here. / Come here. You’re shaking.
[122] ── SCENE: The Grain Room ──
[123] ¶ They do not make it to a feast. The grain-room lamp is closer than pride.
[124] Jumong: Hey. / Numbers later. / Your throat’s brighter than the lamp. Sorry. Not sorry.
[125] Sosuno: I am not your wife yet. / Don’t— my hands. / Counting hand or me. / …Big idiot. / It’s not like that.
[126] Jumong: From the first look. / Buyeo was a hall’s idea. This one’s mine. / Give me your mouth… first. / Country later.
[127] Sosuno: Then take it. / Don’t put a price on it. / I already lost the count.
[128] Sosuno: Now come here before I take it back.
[129] ¶ She hits his chest, once, not hard enough. Then she is on his mouth like she is angry at it.
[130] ¶ The dusty-rose hiked, she braces against the sacks with her back to him, pulls him in by the collar and tells him she hates him in the same breath. Then she feels the weight of him, and the hate gets specific. Love and spite in one grip.
[131] Sosuno: It won’t— ah— fit—
[132] Jumong: Hate me then. / Harder. / God you’re— look at you.
[133] Sosuno: Look— look at you— that chest— that back— those hips I watched from the loft— / That sound. Wet. Slap. That’s— that’s Little Sosuno, she’s— ah— dripping, she— / Take it. That sexy— man meat— I said take it and— destroy my tight little ass— / Beat her up. Beat up Little Sosuno till she’s just wet. Nothing left. That’s all she is—
[134] Jumong: Little Sosuno. / Cute. / I’ve got both of you.
